body:
Measured on the running cloud ALB pod 2026-07-27, while investigating the DiskPressure incident that wedged a node for four days.

## The measurement

`site-packages` on the ALB pod is **8.2 GB**. Its largest entries:

```
4.3G  nvidia          <- CUDA runtime libraries
1.7G  torch
639M  triton
152M  pyarrow
117M  lancedb
115M  opencv_python.libs
```

**6.6 GB — 80% of the tree — is the GPU stack.**

## Why that is wrong here

The pod it installs on cannot use any of it:

```
node           ip-100-64-8-228  /  m7i-flex.large
GPU capacity   none declared
/dev/nvidia*   absent from the container
torch build    2.10.0+cu128     <- CUDA 12.8
```

`m7i-flex.large` is a general-purpose CPU instance. There is no GPU on the node, no device in the container, and no CUDA driver for those libraries to bind to. They are downloaded, unpacked and written to disk on **every pod start**, and never executed.

This is also independently settled: **the ALB holds no models** — inference goes out to the H100 behind `model.rocketride.dev` (`--modelserver=wss://…` is in the pod's own command line). Nothing here was ever meant to run on a GPU.

## Where it comes from

No node declares `torch`. It arrives transitively through four:

```
anonymize   embedding_video   preprocessor_langchain   embedding_image
```

via `sentence-transformers` / `transformers` / GLiNER-style packages. PyPI's default `torch` wheel is the CUDA build, so a plain resolve pulls `nvidia-*` and `triton` with it. **No CPU index is configured anywhere** — checked across all 103 node requirement files and the Dockerfiles.

## The fix

Resolve `torch` from the PyTorch CPU index so the CUDA wheels are never selected:

```
--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
torch==2.10.0+cpu
```

`torch+cpu` is roughly 200 MB and pulls **no** `nvidia-*` packages.

Expected effect on the ALB, using tonight's numbers:

```
site-packages   8.2 GB -> ~1.8 GB
pod total      16.8 GB -> ~2 GB   (with the 8.6 GB uv cache removed by saas #399)
node usage        84%  -> ~15-20%
```

That does not merely relieve DiskPressure — it removes the condition that produced it.

## Caveats, stated rather than glossed

- **This is the right default for the cloud, not necessarily for every target.** A self-hosted user with a GPU wants the CUDA build. The CPU index belongs on the cloud image build, or behind a build arg — not hardcoded into node requirements in a way that silently disables GPU inference for OSS users.
- **Verify the four nodes still work** on `torch+cpu` before shipping. They should — they call the model server rather than computing locally — but "should" is not "did", and this is exactly the kind of change that looks free and is not.
- Belongs with the centralised constraints work (task #109 / #1098): the same lockfile that pins versions is the natural place to pin the index.

Related: rocketride-saas #396, #397, #399.

Addendum — my own filing was incomplete, found while verifying the "should work on CPU" claim I made in it.

**There is a second GPU source, and it is declared explicitly rather than pulled transitively.** `nodes/src/nodes/anonymize/requirements.txt`:

```
onnxruntime-gpu==1.20.1; platform_system != 'Darwin'
onnxruntime==1.20.1;     platform_system == 'Darwin'
```

The marker keys on **operating system**, not on whether a GPU exists. Every non-Mac install therefore gets the GPU build — including a `m7i-flex.large` with no GPU and no `/dev/nvidia*`. The intent was presumably "Macs have no CUDA", which is true but is not the same statement as "everything else does".

**Current state on the pod, checked rather than assumed:** `onnxruntime*` is **not** in site-packages right now. `depends()` installs per node on demand and the anonymize node has not run on this pod. So:

- the 4.3 GB `nvidia/` tree measured above is **entirely torch's** — `cudnn`, `cublas`, `cusparselt`, `cufft` are its dependency set;
- `onnxruntime-gpu` is a **latent** second helping that lands the first time anyone runs the anonymize node.

**Consequence for the fix:** pointing torch at the CPU index is necessary but **not sufficient**. `onnxruntime-gpu` would still be installed on demand and drag its own CUDA/cuDNN. The marker needs to select GPU on GPU-bearing targets rather than on "not a Mac" — a build arg or an environment-driven requirement, in the same place as the torch index.

Correcting this here rather than quietly editing the issue body: I wrote "no node declares torch" and that is true, but I then generalised it to "the GPU stack is entirely transitive", which is not. One of the four nodes asks for a GPU runtime by name and I did not read far enough before saying otherwise.

Resolution tested, so the "should work on CPU" in the body is no longer a guess at the dependency level.

Ran `uv pip compile` over the four nodes' combined requirements, targeting `x86_64-manylinux2014` / cp312 — the platform the ALB installs for:

```
DEFAULT INDEX (what prod resolves today)
  packages resolved : 119
  nvidia-* packages : 13
  torch             : 2.6.0

PYTORCH CPU INDEX  (--extra-index-url .../whl/cpu, torch pinned +cpu)
  packages resolved : 105
  nvidia-* packages : 0
  torch             : 2.6.0+cpu
```

**The resolution succeeds with no conflicts**, and all thirteen CUDA packages disappear:

```
nvidia-cublas-cu12   nvidia-cuda-cupti-cu12   nvidia-cuda-nvrtc-cu12
nvidia-cuda-runtime-cu12   nvidia-cudnn-cu12   nvidia-cufft-cu12
nvidia-curand-cu12   nvidia-cusolver-cu12   nvidia-cusparse-cu12
nvidia-cusparselt-cu12   nvidia-nccl-cu12   nvidia-nvjitlink-cu12
nvidia-nvtx-cu12
```

Fourteen fewer packages, and the entire CUDA tree gone — nothing in `gliner`, `transformers`, `accelerate`, `langchain` or `tokenizers` requires the GPU build to satisfy its constraints.

**What this does and does not establish.** It proves the dependency graph is satisfiable on CPU — the part that could have blocked the whole idea, and the cheapest thing to have checked first. It does **not** prove the four nodes behave correctly at runtime; `torch+cpu` raises at the point CUDA is actually requested rather than at import, so a functional run of anonymize / embedding_image / embedding_video / preprocessor_langchain is still required before this ships. I would not treat a green resolve as permission to skip that.

Also unchanged by this test: the `onnxruntime-gpu` marker in the comment above. That is a separate declaration and this resolve did not include it.

**Correcting my own diagnosis in this issue — the cause is simpler and more deliberate than I described.**

I wrote that torch "arrives transitively via gliner/transformers/accelerate" and that "no CPU index is configured anywhere (checked all 103 node requirement files + Dockerfiles)". Both halves are wrong, and the second explains the first: I scanned **node** requirement files. The pin lives in a **common** one.

### `packages/ai/src/ai/common/torch/requirements.txt`

```
# Install pytorch and its requirements
# The --extra-index-url allow us to load the gpu version. This will
# work on the cpu if cuda or gpu is not available
#
--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
torch==2.10.0 ; platform_system == 'Darwin' and platform_machine == 'arm64'
torch==2.10.0+cu128; platform_system != 'Darwin'
torchvision==0.25.0 ; platform_system == 'Darwin' and platform_machine == 'arm64'
torchvision==0.25.0+cu128 ; platform_system != 'Darwin'
```

torch is **explicitly pinned to `+cu128`**, and a CUDA index is **explicitly configured**. Nothing transitive about it.

### Why it reaches every install, not just GPU nodes

```
REQUIREMENTS_GLOBS = ['requirement*.txt', 'nodes/**/requirement*.txt', 'ai/**/requirement*.txt']
```

`ai/**` matches `ai/common/torch/requirements.txt`, so it is in the combined set on every run. `ensure_constraints()` compiles that set into `constraints.txt` — with `--emit-index-url`, which deliberately preserves the cu128 index — and `_constraints_args()` then applies `-c constraints.txt` to **every** node install. So the pin is global, regardless of which node triggered the resolve.

The live cloud pod runs `torch 2.10.0+cu128`, matching the pin exactly.

### The actual defect

The comment above the pin is true — the CUDA build does run on a CPU-only host — but the selector is `platform_system != 'Darwin'`, which keys on **operating system**, not on whether a GPU exists. Every Linux host gets the CUDA build whether or not it has a GPU, and pays ~6.6 GB (nvidia-* 4.3G + torch 1.7G + triton 639M) for a runtime that is never executed.

That is the same shape as the `onnxruntime-gpu==1.20.1 ; platform_system != 'Darwin'` marker already noted in this issue. Two instances of one mistake: an OS marker standing in for a hardware capability, which is not something a requirements marker can express.

### What this changes about the fix

My earlier suggestion — add a CPU index — was aiming at the wrong layer. There is no index to add; there is a pin to make conditional. And because the pin is correct for a self-hosted user with a GPU, it must not simply be flipped: doing that would silently disable GPU inference for everyone running this engine on their own hardware.

So the selection has to move to a layer that knows the deployment's intent. For our cloud specifically that can be done without touching this file at all — the SaaS image already overlays files onto the engine image, so it can ship a CPU-pinned variant of this one file. That keeps OSS behaviour byte-identical and is what I will pursue for the cloud pods.

Whether the engine itself should grow a first-class way to express "resolve for CPU" is a separate design question, and a better one than anything I proposed above. Flagging rather than deciding.

**Still not verified, and it gates any rollout:** that the four affected nodes actually run on `torch+cpu`. `torch+cpu` raises when CUDA is requested, not at import, so a clean resolve proves nothing. That functional check remains outstanding.

Independently verified the proposed fix's mechanism, since it lands on a production path that already caused a DiskPressure incident. It holds, and the correspondence is exact.

### Resolve comparison

Both resolved with `uv 0.9.16`, targeting `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, CPython 3.12 — no install, resolve only:

| | total pins | `nvidia-*` | `triton` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `torch==2.10.0` (default PyPI) | 28 | **15** | **1** |
| `torch==2.10.0+cpu` (`--extra-index-url .../whl/cpu`) | **10** | 0 | 0 |

So the CPU index drops 16 CUDA-stack packages and 18 pins overall.

### That is exactly what is in the committed lock

`nodes/src/nodes/constraints.lock` carries **16** CUDA-stack pins, all gated `platform_machine == 'x86_64' and sys_platform == 'linux'`. Intersecting them against the default-torch resolve: **16 of 16 match**. The set the CPU index removes is precisely the set the lock currently pins — not an approximation of it.

### Other claims, checked against `develop` @ `b8068d7`

- **"No node declares `torch`"** — confirmed, no direct declaration in any node `requirements.txt`.
- **"No CPU index is configured anywhere"** — confirmed across all node requirements and `docker/`.
- Minor: the count is **104** `requirements.txt` files, not 103.

### One thing that makes the change easier than it looks

`depends.py` already passes `--emit-index-url`, and its own comment says that exists to *"Preserve `--extra-index-url` etc. so install/dry-run can find packages (e.g. `torch+cu128`)"*. The plumbing for a non-default index is already there and already exercised for the CUDA case; what is missing is only the configuration, which supports doing this behind a build arg rather than by editing node requirements.

### What I did not verify

The caveat in this issue is the one that matters and I could not close it:

> Verify the four nodes still work on `torch+cpu` before shipping.

I resolved dependency graphs; I did not execute `anonymize`, `embedding_video`, `preprocessor_langchain`, or `embedding_image` against a CPU-only build. The resolve being clean says the wheels install, not that the nodes behave. Worth noting `sentence-transformers`/GLiNER paths can call `.cuda()` or `device_map='auto'` explicitly, which fails differently from a missing wheel — that is the specific thing I would test before shipping, and it is not something this resolve data covers.

Opened #2003 for this: an opt-in `ROCKETRIDE_TORCH_CPU` flag that resolves torch from the PyTorch CPU wheel index, default off so GPU/self-hosted users are unaffected. Hit this while self-hosting on a CPU-only host. Happy to adjust the approach.

title: ALB installs 6.6 GB of CUDA on a CPU-only node — 80% of its disk is a GPU stack it cannot run
